analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay equally for jobs of equivalent skill, effort, and responsibility, targeting sex and race pay gaps.
analysis.headline: The Fair Pay Act of 2007 was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the federal wage law so that employers could not pay lower wages in jobs dominated by women or by people of a particular race or national origin than they pay for different jobs that require equivalent skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. It went beyond existing law, which only requires equal pay for literally the same work. It added damages, class actions, expert-fee reimbursement for workers who sue, anti-retaliation protections including the right to discuss wages, and new pay-records reporting to the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and people of color working in occupations dominated by their own group, in fields such as caregiving, clerical work, and service jobs, whose pay is often set lower than men's pay in different but comparably demanding jobs. All workers gain a new right to ask about and discuss wages without being fired or punished.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in female- and minority-dominated jobs

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits paying lower wages for a job dominated by one sex, race, or national origin than for another job requiring equivalent skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions — 'equivalent jobs' may be dissimilar but comparably demanding [S3].

The bill's findings cite Census Bureau data that as of 2000 women earned as much as men in only 5 of 400 fields with 10,000+ full-time workers, and a 2004 analysis finding women paid 76 cents per dollar a man makes [S3].

Adds compensatory and punitive damages against violators, allows suits to proceed as class actions, and requires courts to award expert fees to prevailing workers — remedies that make it financially practical for individual workers to sue [S3].
Makes it unlawful to fire, coerce, intimidate, or interfere with an employee for inquiring about, disclosing, or discussing wages — including any other employee's wages [S3].
Protects workers who oppose discriminatory pay or assist an investigation or proceeding under the Act from discharge or other discrimination [S3].

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more after two years) to report wage rates by job classification along with the sex, race, and national origin of employees at each rate, giving the EEOC and the public data on pay gaps; employers may not comply by cutting anyone's wages [S3].

Applies the same pay-equity rules to congressional and executive branch employees through conforming amendments to the Congressional Accountability Act and the Presidential and Executive Office Accountability Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the federal wage-and-hour law would bear the cost of re-examining pay structures across dissimilar jobs, preserving and reporting detailed wage records, and paying back wages plus compensatory and punitive damages in lawsuits, including class actions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers covered by federal wage law

drawbacks.text: The 'equivalent jobs' standard is inherently subjective: deciding whether, say, a nurse's job and a technician's job require equivalent composite skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions invites extensive litigation and depends heavily on EEOC guidelines that courts and employers could contest for years [S3].

Employers would face new administrative burdens — preserving records of how every wage rate is set and filing annual wage reports by race, sex, and national origin — a real compliance cost, particularly for mid-sized firms [S3].

A good-faith objection: pay differences between dissimilar occupations often reflect market supply and demand rather than discrimination, and forcing employers to equalize pay across job titles could push them to restructure or eliminate jobs rather than raise the lower-paid ones. The bill attempts to address this by allowing differentials based on job-related business factors — but lets employees defeat that defense by showing a cheaper alternative practice the employer refused to adopt [S3].

The class action and punitive damages provisions significantly raise employers' litigation exposure, which even supporters would acknowledge is a genuine cost to businesses that is passed on in prices or hiring [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given workers a real remedy for a documented problem — pay differences between comparably demanding jobs that track sex and race — backed by damages, class actions, and wage data that would make gaps visible. The costs are real but ordinary: compliance and litigation expenses for employers, and the inherent difficulty of comparing dissimilar jobs, which the bill manages with a business-necessity defense that workers can rebut. On balance it was a substantial, enforceable pay-equity policy rather than a symbolic one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on April 11, 2007, joined on introduction by 11 other senators including Edward Kennedy, Patty Murray, Barbara Mikulski, Sherrod Brown, Russ Feingold, Barbara Boxer, Patrick Leahy, John Kerry, Bernard Sanders, and Richard Durbin [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill attracted 16 cosponsors — 15 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republicans [S4].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers benefited from avoiding a new pay-equity mandate with damages, class actions, and wage-reporting requirements. Women and people of color in underpaid, occupation-dominated fields got nothing; the pay gap documented in the bill's own findings continued.

for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original sponsor of the bill [S3]; his committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on it [S5].

for.name: 16 senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic and Independent — the sponsor, the 11 senators who joined the introduction, and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders, with no Republican cosponsor; the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so the broader Senate never went on record [S3, S4].

industries.industry: Employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act (businesses, government contractors, and public employers)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to equalize pay across equivalent jobs, keep and file detailed wage records by race, sex, and national origin, and pay back wages plus compensatory and punitive damages in class-action suits. Its interest in the bill's failure ran against the workers whose pay would have risen.
